analytic.title: Thermochemical upcycling of food waste into engineered biochar for energy and environmental applications: A critical review

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Environmental issues caused by food waste are important concerns for human wellbeing and ecosystem health. Valorization of food waste into energy and carbon materials has been extensively investigated. Here, we reviewed the most recent advancements in the thermochemical conversion of food waste into engineered biochar.

Synthesis routes and practical applications of the food waste-derived biochar was succinctly reviewed. Engineered biochar is a promising alternative for mitigating environmental pollution and alleviating energy crisis. The underlying relationships between engineered biochar properties and specific applications are still unclear, therefore, machine learning-aided engineered biochar design and process optimization was proposed. Moreover, before any industrial scale implementation, detailed assessments of the environmental benefits and economic feasibility must be conducted.

In the context of carbon neutrality, thermochemical upcycling of food waste into engineered biochar for energy and environmental applications can significantly contribute to attaining sustainable food waste management, mitigating environmental pollution, and addressing the energy shortage crisis, and thus will eventually facilitate the fulfillment of United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Furthermore, the existing challenges in the practical valorization of food waste into engineered biochar are comprehensively discussed, and outlooks are proposed.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Food waste is a global issue that brings serious environmental, economic and social challenges [1][2][3]. Many countries have taken measures to reduce food waste and sustainable management of food waste separately collected from other wastes.

Collected food waste can be processed to minimize its environmental impact and to maximize its benefits within a circular economy. Food waste, which is mainly composed of organics (i.e., carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and lipids), is hereby converted into high value-added products (e.g., methane, bioethanol, syngas, chemicals, and carbon materials) [4]. Recently, the upcycling of food waste into advanced carbon materials has been considered an emerging paradigm shift from landfilling and incineration. The major upcycling approaches include thermochemical conversions (e.g., hydrothermal carbonization (HTC), pyrolysis, and gasification) and biological conversions (e.g., anaerobic digestion (AD)) [4,5]. AD is extensively investigated for transforming food waste into value-added products, owing to its considerable advantages of cost-effectiveness, mild operating conditions, and relatively low energy consumption [6][7][8][9]. However, AD generally requires a long residence time and a high-quality feedstock [10].

Compared with the biological conversions mentioned above, thermochemical conversion is fast and achieves high yields of value-added products [11]. Pyrolysis, a high-temperature treatment in the absence of free oxygen, requires large amount of energy because of the high moisture content of food waste. To effectively upcycle food waste this way, prior dewatering (or pre-drying) is required. HTC, in contrast, does not require pre-drying and therefore is considered a promising alternative for conversion of food waste into a solid carbon material, commonly termed as hydrochar [11,12]. The main products from slow pyrolysis and HTC are carbon-rich materials referred to as biochar and hydrochar, respectively. These can be further activated and/or modified into engineered biochar with improved properties for various applications. Researchers are currently focusing on developing green, sustainable, and cost-effective thermochemical processes or integrated biological and thermochemical processes to achieve sustainable management of food waste towards a circular economy (Figure 1). Because of the diversity and complexity of food waste, feedstock-specific process technologies are required for the treatment of food waste in biorefineries [13,14]. The solid carbon residue that cannot be further biologically decomposed or chemically extracted normally accounts for a large proportion of processed food waste. These residues can be converted into solid biochar, liquid bio-oil, and gaseous products via hydrothermal conversion or pyrolysis. So far, only a few papers have reviewed the thermochemical conversion of food waste, focusing on the operating conditions, reaction mechanisms, product distributions, and evolution pathways. In particular, the gaseous and liquid products derived from various food wastes have been extensively investigated [15][16][17][18] in comparison to the solid biochar products. For example, Pham et al. [15] reviewed food waste-to-energy technologies involving biological conversion using AD or fermentation, and thermochemical processes including pyrolysis, incineration, hydrothermal oxidation, and gasification. Current state-of-the-art in the pyrolysis and gasification of food waste was reviewed by Su et al. [17], Murugesan et al. [18], and Makkawi et al. [19].

This review focuses on food waste-derived engineered biochar for environmental and energy applications, including major and emerging production routes, use of machine learning (ML) in the manufacturing of application-targeted engineered biochar, and practical applications in environmental and energy fields. Physical, chemical, and integrated methods are used to activate (i.e., developing new pores and controlling pore size distributions) and/or modify (i.e., doping surface functional groups) biochar into engineered biochar with wide applications, such as solid fuels, adsorbents (e.g., for CO2 capture), and advanced catalysts (e.g., for electrochemical energy storage and conversion). The review sheds light on the sustainable upcycling of food waste into engineered biochar with high-performance applications and ultimately promotes their large-scale deployment, significantly providing benefits and guidelines to researchers from both academies and industries working in the areas of sustainable valorization of solid waste, climate change mitigation, renewable fuels, energy conversion and storage, and circular carbon economy. In the context of carbon neutrality, sustainable management of food waste will contribute to climate change mitigation, use of renewable alternative fuels and thus contribute to achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

div.head: Hydrothermal conversion
div.p: Hydrothermal conversion (HTC) allows for the synthesis of value-added carbon materials and the recovery of energy from waste with high moisture content [20,21].

HTC at relatively low temperature (180-265 °C) and low pressure (subcritical conditions, up to 6.0 MPa) is favorable for hydrochar production [12,22]. It avoids the requirement for a pre-drying treatment, involves rather mild operating conditions, and features high operational feasibility and relatively low energy consumption [4,11,23,24]. HTC can recover nutrients and fatty acids in liquid food waste, which can be recirculated during processing [25][26][27]. The range of processes involved in hydrochar formation are schematized in Figure 2. The chemical composition of food waste is complex. Lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates are the main component groups. During HTC, subcritical water promotes the hydrolysis of lipids, polysaccharides, and proteins into oligomers and monomers [28,29]. The decomposition of proteins requires a temperature of at least 150 °C but needs to be at least 220 °C if the protein content is above 30 wt.% [28]. Protein hydrolysis is slower than carbohydrate hydrolysis because of the higher stability of peptide bonds compared to glycosidic bonds.

Researchers widely investigated specific mechanisms involved in the HTC of food waste [29,30]. The HTC of complex food waste involved three key reactions: carbonization of carbohydrates, Maillard reaction, and amidation reaction [29]. Lipids play a crucial role in hydrochar formation by inhibiting interactions between carbohydrates and proteins. Carbohydrates play a key role when proteins boost their N-heterocyclic functional groups. Because lipid hydrolysates sorb on the surface of the hydrochar, , the lipids present in the food-waste do not interfere in the process of carbonization [31].

div.head: Pyrolysis
div.p: Compared with HTC mentioned-above, pyrolysis is the thermal degradation of organic materials into carbon-rich by products at a moderate temperature (300-800 °C) and low pressure with little or no available oxygen. A range of atmospheres can be used to ensure anaerobic conditions, including inert gases such as nitrogen, argon, or helium; reactive gases such as carbon dioxide or steam; or vacuum. The properties of the products based on pyrolysis of a given feedstock are mainly influenced by the operating conditions, such as the type of inert gas, flow rate of carrier gas, temperature, heating rate and residence time [32][33][34][35].

Pyrolysis has several advantages. It yields different useful output products (as liquid, solid, and gas), is environmentally friendly and the technology is mature. The yields and properties of the target products can be optimized by adjusting the operating conditions [36].

Various mechanisms are involved in the pyrolysis of food waste. Glucose is one of the most abundant monosaccharides in food waste. During pyrolysis, a dehydration reaction converts glucose into anhydrosugars, which in turn are converted to sorbitol and 1,4-sorbitan through reduction and dehydration, respectively, and subsequently into isosorbide [37]. Via decarbonylation, decarboxylation, and fragmentation reactions, glycerol can be converted into acids, esters, alcohols, hydrocarbons, and alicyclic compounds. The decomposition of steroids generates hydrocarbons [38].

Amine and diketopiperazine species are produced during the pyrolysis of proteins. Amine species are produced via the breakage of peptide bonds, while diketopiperazine species are generated because of the cyclization of amino acids [39].

To date, investigations of the food waste pyrolysis mechanisms have mostly focused on the individual components. However, the interactions between the different components in food waste during pyrolysis remains to be investigated.

Direct pyrolysis of food waste with high water content would, while technically feasible, require considerable energy input for the drying pretreatment, and evaporation of remaining water. Therefore, integrated conversion systems, e.g., AD + pyrolysis; HTC + pyrolysis, have been developed [40][41][42]. Both AD and HTC readily reduce the water content (especially bound water) from food waste by destroying the cell walls [43]. More importantly, AD recovers valuable biogas and nutrients (digestate) from food waste with high water content. The solid residue of AD can then be pyrolyzed for the co-production of biochar and biofuels (e.g., syngas) (Figure 3).

The pyrolysis of solid AD residue from food waste has increasingly been a topic of research [44][45][46]. Zhao et al. [44] compared the pyrolysis of food waste and pyrolysis of its solid digestate. Organic matter of food waste was partially consumed during AD. The pyrolytic gas from food waste was of better quality than that of the residue of AD because its lower heating value (LHV) was high. Higher LHV fuels are generally more efficient and effective for use as energy sources, as they can generate more heat per unit of fuel. This means that they require less fuel to generate the same amount of energy as lower LHV fuels, making them more cost-effective and environmentally friendly. In contrast, the bio-oil and biochar derived from the solid digestate showed better qualities as liquid fuel and as a media for CO2 adsorption.. Pyrolysis of the solid digestate generated fewer N-containing pollutants, indicating that AD coupled with pyrolysis is a more environmentally friendly approach for treating food waste [47].

div.head: Development of engineered biochar derived from food waste
Activation to engineered biochar
div.p: Biochar and hydrochar have a limited surface area and pore structure, and unspecified functional groups [34,48]. Activation treatment aims to improve the textural properties of biochar and hydrochar by creating and/or digging out the internal porous structure in order to broaden the practical applications in environmental protection and energy storage/conversion [48][49][50].

Generally, activation treatments are categorized as physical and chemical. In physical activation, CO2, steam, and air at high operating temperatures (up to 1,000 °C) are widely used [11,51]. Physical activation is a relatively eco-friendly and cost-effective approach for increasing textural properties (i.e., porosity). Among these postmodification treatments, physical activation exhibits lower global warming potential than chemical activation [52]. Steam and CO2, both endothermically react with carbon via two major reactions: 𝐶 + 𝐶𝑂 2 → 2𝐶𝑂, ∆𝐻 = 159𝑘𝐽𝑚𝑜𝑙 -1 ; 𝐶 + 𝐻 2 𝑂 → 𝐶𝑂 + 𝐻 2 , ∆𝐻 = 119𝑘𝐽𝑚𝑜𝑙 -1 [51]. Steam activation effectively improves the porosity and increases the number of O-functional groups on the surface of engineered biochar [53]. Due to its easy handling and low reactivity even at operating temperatures higher than 700 °C, CO2 gas has become the preferred activating agent, making activation easier to control [54,55]. However, in the context of carbon neutrality, CO2 emissions from CO2 activation are an issue. When the surface area, total pore volume, and yield of biochar are low, it means that the biochar may be less effective at removing carbon from the atmosphere and storing it in the soil. This can result in a larger carbon footprint and may offset the potential benefits of using biochar as a carbon sequestration method . Although the surface area, total pore volume, and yield of engineered biochar are generally less than 1,000 m 2 /g, 0.7 cm 3 /g, and 30%, respectively, after physical activation [48,56], the approach has several key advantages, including minimal corrosion to the activating reactor, high deployment feasibility and low production and operating costs, showing a broad commercial potential of engineered biochar-based practical applications.

For chemical activation, either acids (e.g., H3PO4, HNO3, and H2O2), bases (e.g., KOH and NaOH) or salts (e.g., K2CO3, ZnCl2, and MgCl2) are used. These are impregnated on the biochar or hydrochar before chemical activation is performed under an inert gas atmosphere [11,57]. Porosity is directly influenced by the volume of the chemical agent used and the activation temperature. Compared with physical activation, chemical activation has the advantages of low energy consumption due to the low activation temperature and short activation time, and high porosity and yield of the produced engineered biochar. However, issues include intensive chemical corrosion of the reactor during activation, the need for wastewater treatment due to the production of chemically contaminated wastewater, and the extra energy required for subsequent drying of the produced carbon materials. KOH activation is one of the most common and best ways to produce well-developed porous engineered biochar. In a study engineered biochar was synthesized using KOH activation from water chestnut shells [58], achieving a surface area of 3,401 m 3 /g and a total pore volume of 2.50 cm 3 /g. However, KOH activation has considerable environmental impacts, including greenhouse gas emissions from activation and high-water consumption for the impregnation before activation and the washing after activation. The environmental impacts need to be fully assessed from a life-cycle perspective when designing a sustainable and feasible activation technique [59].

div.head: Modification of surface functional group
div.p: In addition to good textural properties, the presence of surface functional groups, such as O-, N-, and S-rich groups, critically determines the potential application performance of engineered biochar [60]. For example, surface O-functional groups (e.g. -OH and -COOH) dramatically improve the adsorption capacity for capturing CO2 and removal of metal contaminants from wastewater [61,62]. Functional groups can be doped on the surface of engineered biochar through various modifications [48,63]. To increase the oxygenated functional groups (e.g., carboxyl and phenolic hydroxyl), surface oxidation, most commonly with H2O2 and HNO3, is most commonly used [63,64]; surface amination, e.g., through high-temperature ammonia (NH3) treatment, can be used to increase amino groups [65]; surface sulfonation can be achieved using concentrated sulfuric acid. In addition to these single-heteroatom doping treatments, dual-or tri-doping treatments are used to enrich surface active sites and enhancing performance during application via synergistic effects. For example, N and S dual-doping is suited for producing engineered biochar for oxygen reduction reactions (ORRs), rechargeable lithium-oxygen batteries, and supercapacitors [66][67][68][69].In addition, the main advantage of food waste-derived engineered biochar materials is the production of porous carbon, self-doped with heteroatoms (e.g., O, N, S) due to the presence of protein (Table 1). Machine learning (ML), an artificial intelligence approach, is promising as a practical alternative to laboratory experiments and computational simulations (e.g., density functional theory and Grand canonical Monte Carlo) for designing and optimizing advanced materials [70]. Several major advantages of ML include efficient screening of large amounts of data within a short time (at the 10 -2 s level), accurate prediction of material properties, and effective identification of the inherent relationship between material properties and specific applications [71]. Recently, ML has been extensively used to accelerate carbon material discovery and elucidate the inherent relationships with their properties and specific applications.

Most of work on ML focused on the forward prediction of target features based on collected datasets of input features by established models within acceptable or reasonable accuracy levels (R 2 > 0.8) [70][71][72][73][74][75]. For example, Yuan et al. [71] applied ML to predict CO2 adsorption performance using biomass waste-derived carbon materials, and Li et al. [73] applied ML to predict and optimize the properties of hydrochar derived from high-moisture municipal solid waste. .
In addition to forward prediction, ML algorithms are also powerful for supporting inverse design, greatly facilitating a paradigm shift towards a closed-loop guideline .

In the context of machine learning and inverse design, closed-loop guidelines involve a continuous feedback loop between the design process and the performance evaluation of the resulting designs [48,76]. Through synthesis and validation, ML algorithms enable guided experiments to discover food waste-derived biochar functional materials with feedstock properties. When integrating computational simulations with experimental validation, ML algorithms can accelerate the synthesis of biochar functional materials derived from food waste targeted toward a specific application.

Since ML is a data-driven approach, consistent data formatting (i.e., unit consistency) is an essential step in the process. Missing data is a critical issue when performing ML-aided investigations. Generally, each piece of data consists of valid values for all input variables, and those with unsolved missing data are discarded. Sometimes, the missing data issue can be solved by data imputation, i.e., replacing the missing values with estimates. Most data are manually extracted from recent publications, which are both time-and labor-consuming. Therefore, it is desirable to create open databases with standard formats to accelerate the ML-based discovery of food waste-derived advanced materials and their potential applications.

div.head: Practical applications of food waste-derived engineered biochar
div.p: Engineered biochar produced from food waste has broad applications, including solid fuels, adsorbents for environmental remediation (e.g., CO2 capture), and electrochemical applications (e.g., energy storage and conversion) [11,47,78]. Food waste-derived hydrochar produced via HTC has been widely developed for direct use as solid fuels. Moreover, hydrochar produced from the HTC and pyrolysis of food waste can be activated and/or modified to obtain high-performance engineered biochar for energy and environmental applications.

div.head: Solid fuels
div.p: Because food waste is mainly composed of organic components (i.e., carbohydrates, protein, and lipids), it has good potential for producing solid fuel with a relatively high heating value. Currently, significant efforts have been taken to produce solid fuels from food waste via HTC [79,80]. Theppitak et al. [80] compared the pyrolysis and HTC of food waste for solid fuel production. Compared with the biochar produced via HTC, that produced via pyrolysis at temperatures higher than 300 °C showed superior fuel properties, with a high heating value and high fixed carbon content. When the moisture content of the food waste is high (i.e., >75%), the HTC process is more suitable and economically efficient. Moreover, the HTC process removes protein from food waste and simultaneously increases the yield of biochar with a higher heating value due to the carbohydrate-rich fraction. The HTC process also resolves issues related to the heterogeneity of mixed food waste [81]. However, the impacts of factors such as biochar palletization, gas composition, NOx emission and by-product utilization in the following thermochemical process (i.e., combustion) should be considered [82,83]. Su et al. [24] recently studied the conversion of food waste (after extracting oil) into solid fuel by the HTC process in a large-scale plant (200 t/d). Most food wastes are composed of carbohydrates, protein, and lipids, making them suitable for the production of solid fuels with a high heating value.

Compared with other biomass wastes such as agroforestry residues, food waste also has a lower ash content, especially of alkali and alkaline earth minerals, which may reduce sintering and corrosivity. However, food waste has a high moisture content, so developing a cost-effective dewatering pre-treatment remains a key challenge for advancing practical applications. Moreover, the co-production of oil fuels and biogas can greatly improve the technical-and economic feasibility of converting food waste into energy products.

div.head: CO2 adsorption
div.p: In the context of carbon neutrality, carbon capture is essential to mitigate climate change [84] owing to the current high atmospheric CO2 concentration (up to 420 ppm) and the increasing annual growth rate of CO2 (up to 2.4 ppm per year) [85].

Carbon capture, alternatively known as greenhouse gas removal or CO2 removal mainly addresses CO2 removal from large point-emission sources (e.g., power plants and cement industries) and even from the atmosphere (i.e., direct air capture) [86].

Among the available technical approaches, CO2 adsorption is widely considered a promising and feasible route owing to its mild operating conditions, cost-effectiveness (especially when using solid waste as a precursor for adsorbent synthesis), high feasibility for commercial-scale application, and low energy consumption [11,48].

The circular economy-inspired upcycling of food waste into novel carbon materials for CO2 adsorption followed by soil remediation has been proposed with the potential of achieving negative carbon emissions [59], representing a sustainable waste-toresource strategy that simultaneously mitigates climate change. Moreover, surplus electricity, engineered biochar material and captured CO2 gas can be generated in a sustainable and multifunctional food waste-based system that integrates temperature swing CO2 adsorption to reach zero carbon emissions. No waste is generated in this circular life-cycle system, which is beneficial for achieving UN Sustainable Development Goals 11 (sustainable cities and communities), 12 (responsible consumption and production), and 13 (climate action). Engineered biochar for CO2 adsorption is expected to have a high CO2 adsorption capacity, low energy requirement for regeneration, excellent cyclic stability, high selectivity for CO2 over other gases, and fast kinetic characteristics for adsorption-desorption cycles [48,87].

The CO2 uptake versus the surface area of food waste (e.g., fruit waste, vegetable waste, shrimp shells, coconut shells, and spent coffee grounds)-derived engineered biochar for CO2 adsorption is investigated [59,88,89], illustrating two major findings. First, through effective synthesis routes, most food waste-derived engineered biochar materials have a viable CO2 capture performance of more than 3 mol/kg at 25 °C (1 bar), in accordance with the US National Energy Technology Laboratory criterion for applicable and practical CO2 capture. Second, the relationship between CO2 uptake and Brunauer-Emmett-Teller surface area (SBET) is not linear, suggesting that CO2 uptake does not exhibit a directly proportional relationship with SBET.

However, when plotting CO2 uptake versus SBET for materials with pores smaller than β nm (Sβ, refers to the surface area of the narrow pores under β nm in diameter), an excellent linear relationship was observed between CO2 uptake and S0.8, implying that the performance of food waste-derived engineered biochar materials for CO2 adsorption is significantly mediated by the surface area, limited by narrow pores smaller than 0.8 nm at 25 °C (1 bar) [59,90]. In a case study , spent coffee grounds were upcycled into engineered biochar with a high-performance CO2 adsorption capacity of 4.54 mol/kg at 25 °C (1 bar) via simple and sustainable synthesis routes [89], demonstrating the great potential for commercial-scale food waste conversion for CO2 capture applications.

Before globally deploying CO2 adsorption techniques using food waste-derived engineer biochar materials as adsorbents, several existing challenges or barriers must be addressed. First, CO2 selectivity over other gases (e.g., N2) is a critical factor in the potential performance of commercial-scale CO2 adsorption [91,92]. To the best of our knowledge, food waste-derived engineered biochar materials have relatively low CO2 selectivity, which could result in low CO2 purity when evaluating cyclic performance using pressure temperature swing or temperature vacuum swing CO2 adsorption [91].

Moreover, low CO2 purity products would require further gas sorption and separation treatments to obtain high-purity CO2 gas for sustainable and practical CO2 utilization, dramatically increasing the investment for CO2 capture. Therefore, to produce engineered biochar with high selectivity towards CO2 remains an important topic of research.

Second, integrating ML to guide high-performance CO2 adsorbent preparation is considered a promising route to accelerate the deployment of practical CO2 adsorption applications [93]. However, thus far, only CO2 adsorption capacity has been predicted

through ML [71,94]. Other critical indicators, especially CO2 selectivity, also need to be incorporated into ML models. In addition, following the inverse design perspective, the low CO2 selectivity issue might be solved via several iterations of ML model development and experimental validation [95].

Third, environmental impact and economic feasibility are the key factors to assess the emerging CO2 adsorption technologies from both life cycle and techno-economic perspectives [53,59]. Interdisciplinary collaboration between material science, data science, thermochemical engineering, and environmental engineering researchers is required for developing adequate advanced CO2 adsorption systems using food wastederived engineered biochar materials.

div.head: Energy storage and conversion
div.p: N-doped engineered biochar materials show particularly high potential for electrochemical applications [78,96]. Table 2 shows examples of the preparation, properties, and performance of engineered biochar materials derived from various food wastes, for electrochemical applications including supercapacitors, batteries, ORRs, and hydrogen evolution reactions (HERs). In general, the electrochemical performance of these engineered biochar materials is influenced by the textural structure (e.g., hierarchical porous structure), specific surface area, heteroatom (e.g., N, S, P, and O) doping, and active metal (e.g., transition metal) loading. Accordingly, these parameters depend on the feedstock type and activation/modification methods used. Carbon materials possessing high specific surface areas, hierarchical porous structure, multiple heteroatom-doping, and metal catalyst loading have been shown to exhibit high electrochemical performance. In particular, hierarchical engineered biochar materials synthesized from food waste have been developed for supercapacitor applications (Table 2). Even in the absence of metal catalysts, the maximum capacitance can reach 476,000 F/kg, with high cycling stability (90.9% of the original capacitance retained after 10,000 cycles at 1,000 A/kg current density) [97]. This high performance is attributed to the properties of fishbone, which is mainly composed of protein (N, S, and C source) and CaCO3 (self-template), thereby producing N-and S-doped engineered biochar. The selection of a suitable type of food waste is important for the synthesis of functional carbon materials. For example, shrimp shell composed of chitin (N and C source) and inorganic CaCO3 (selftemplate) may be suited to produce N-doped engineered biochar [98][99][100]. Gao et al.
[98] prepared N-doped hierarchical engineered biochar from shrimp shells containing abundant mineral scaffold (CaCO3) as a self-template combined with KOH activation.

Shrimp shells were first activated by KOH in an Ar atmosphere to produce micropores at 700 °C, and then the CaCO3 was removed using acetic acid to form hierarchical engineered biochar, which exhibited a high specific capacitance of 348,000 F/kg in a 6 M KOH electrolyte. Wang et al. [100] synthesized a N and P codoped engineered biochar material embedded with bimetallic phosphide (FeCoP2@NPPC), via a sol-gel and carbonization (N2, 900 °C) process using sustainable N-and P-enriched chitosan and transition metal salts as precursors.

FeCoP2@NPPC had good catalytic activities in HERs, oxygen evolution reactions and overall water splitting. It requires low overpotential between 114 to 150 mV at a current density of 10 mA/cm 2 for HERs in 0.5 M H2SO4 and 1.0 M KOH, while the overpotential of 236 mV for OER in 1.0 M KOH solution. The FeCoP2@NPPC material was capable of transferring electrons and electrolytes and increasing the contact area of the active sites and electrolytes. More importantly, the wettability and conductivity of engineered biochar can be improved by doping N-and P-containing functionalities.

Currently, viable methods in developing carbon materials from food waste for electrochemical applications are still in an early phase of development. The diversity of food waste and the high cost of synthesis processes significantly limit the largescale application of waste conversion technologies. Therefore, achieving full valorization of food waste into biofuels, chemicals, and high value-added carbon materials remains an important challenge requiring further investigation. In addition, techno-economic and life-cycle assessments of the integrated processes based on the characteristics of various food wastes are necessary to meet the industrial requirements for large-scale processing.

div.head: Conclusions and outlook
div.p: Thermochemical conversions are a promising route for upcycling food waste into high value-added fuels and advanced carbon materials due to the short residence times required, high yields of a wide range of products, high conversion efficiencies and feasible deployment for practical applications. Numerous research focused on optimizing thermochemical reaction conditions. . This review summarizes the processes of producing biochar and hydrochar via the slow pyrolysis and HTC of food waste and their by-products. Engineered biochar synthesis through activation (i.e., physical and chemical) and surface modifications (i.e., O-, N-, and S-doping) can be further optimized using ML approaches. Moreover, practical applications of engineered biochar, such as solid fuels, adsorbents (i.e., CO2 adsorption), and advanced catalytic conversions (i.e., electrochemical catalysis), were thoroughly reviewed.

Food waste is a promising and sustainable alternative to solid fuels. It is often characterized by high-water content. HTC enables the direct conversion of food waste into hydrochar for solid fuel applications. Compared with other biomass waste, such as agroforestry residues, food waste has a lower ash content, especially of alkali and alkaline earth minerals, which is beneficial for reducing both sintering and corrosive risks during thermochemical conversions. However, because of the high moisture content, developing a low-cost and efficient dewatering pre-treatment remains a key challenge. The co-production of bio-oil fuels (from waste cooking oil) and biogas (from AD pre-treatment) dramatically increases both the technical and economic feasibility of thermochemical upcycling.

Biochar and hydrochar can be activated and/or modified into advanced engineered biochar materials for energy and environmental applications. Owing to its stable physicochemical properties, tunable pore structures, effective surface functional groups and cost-effectiveness, engineered biochar has been widely synthesized into advanced carbon materials for adsorption and electrochemical applications. In the context of carbon neutrality, paradigm shifts to interdisciplinary collaboration are urgently needed to achieve the circular economy of food waste. For example, material science, data science, thermochemical engineering, and environmental engineering are the basic requirements for developing an advanced CO2 adsorption system using food waste-derived engineered biochar. Moreover, the wide range of feedstocks and lack of synthesis guidelines for engineered biochar greatly limit its commercial applications.

A powerful ML approach has been considered a promising route for synthesizing high-performance engineered biochar. ML can be used not only to accurately predict practical performance using engineered biochar but also to efficiently provide inverse design guidelines to synthesis engineered biochar for a specific application. In addition, both environmental benefits and economic feasibility need to be verified using techno-economic and life-cycle assessments before food waste-derived engineered biochar can be synthesized and applied on an industrial scale.
To increase application of food waste-derived engineered biochar materials, several efforts need to be made in the future as follows:

(1) AD is still the dominant pre-treatment for sustainable food waste management into methane and solid residue because it has a better techno-economic feasibility compared with the direct thermochemical processes (e.g., pyrolysis, gasification).

However, it is still necessary to perform thermochemical routes for further upcycling solid residue into high value-added engineered biochar materials. In the future, more efforts should be made towards integrating AD and thermochemical processing.

(2) For the application of food waste-derived engineered biochar as an adsorbent, most of the current research has focused on removal of conventional pollutants (e.g., VOCs adsorption, CO₂ capture). There is scope to use food waste-derived engineered biochar with functionalized properties for treatment of emerging contaminants.

(3) Many investigations have been performed in the conversion of diverse food waste to biochar materials for solid biofuel productions or carbon material applications, but these studies mainly focused on the optimization of processing and utilizing conditions. To date, less work has been done on the techno-economic and life-cycle assessment of the whole process including biofuels and production and application of carbon materials.
